summary:
I've been building Keikochō, a Japanese-learning dashboard that generates its own kana drills instead of relying on Anki or Duolingo. The interesting constraint was that I'm a true beginner myself, so the app had to be honest about what a learner actually knows versus what they've just recognized with help — cued answers (tap-to-select with audio on every tile) get logged separately from unassisted recall, and only unassisted recall ever counts toward "mastered." That distinction caught a real bug: an early version was letting words unlock into the drill queue that contained a kana the learner hadn't actually learned yet, so I rewrote the segmentation logic to check real per-character progress instead of trusting the word list.

Text-to-speech turned into its own project. I switched the Japanese audio pipeline from one TTS engine to another (VOICEVOX) specifically because it exposes an editable pronunciation layer — you can inspect and patch the phonetic reading before synthesizing, which matters when the model gets a reading wrong in a way that would silently teach the wrong sound. I added a build-time check that verifies every generated clip's reading against what was intended, and it's already caught real mispronunciations before they shipped.

On the infrastructure side, I run a small local LLM setup (a shared GPU box) that multiple tools compete for — SillyTavern, ComfyUI, a few side projects. I wrote a proxy that serializes access to the card and swaps models in and out on demand, since only one can really live in VRAM at a time. The most satisfying fix there was around keeping a large model "warm": the naive version paid a multi-minute penalty on the first request after eviction because the whole context had to be reprocessed from scratch. I ended up saving and restoring the model's internal cache state directly, so a warm reload comes back in seconds instead of minutes.

I also picked up an existing open-source VTT (virtual tabletop) project and forked it into a proper workflow — origin/upstream/fork split so I can track the original repo's changes while sending my own patches upstream as pull requests, rather than drifting into an unmergeable fork.

highlights.oneLiner: Proxy serializing GPU access across tools; added KV cache save/restore so warm reloads take seconds, not minutes
